section_summary: This section contains translated monitoring transcripts of Japanese station JZI broadcasts from December 1941 and January 1942. The broadcasts report Japanese military operations across East and Southeast Asia and present Japan’s account of the war against Britain and the United States. Later documents concern interference with Japanese broadcasts in Brazil, reports of radio signals heard in Mexico, and diplomatic assessments of Japanese broadcasts about German advances against the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 21, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast describes the Japan–Thailand alliance and Japanese claims of advances around Penang, the Philippines, and Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: The transcript gives treaty terms and statements by Tōgō and Tōjō, then reports claimed Japanese landings, naval sinkings, and bombing. The monitor notes severe interference during parts of the broadcast.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 22, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast claims Japanese gains in the Philippines, Malaya, and Hong Kong and reviews the first two weeks of war.
subfiles.summary: Reports include new Luzon landings, attacks on Singapore and Hong Kong, and extensive claims about U.S. fleet losses at Hawaii. It also covers the Thailand alliance, Axis celebrations in Tokyo, and a meeting of the Nippon–Burma society.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 23, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports operations in Luzon, Mindanao, Malaya, and Hong Kong and argues for a prolonged war against Britain and the United States.
subfiles.summary: The transcript claims continuing Japanese advances, major Allied naval losses, and limited Japanese losses. It denies reports of a Japanese occupation of Macau, discusses China and submarine warfare, and presents an extended account of Allied bases and Japan’s strategic rationale for war.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 24, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast announces the capture of Wake Island and Davao and reports fighting in Malaya, Burma, Hong Kong, and Luzon.
subfiles.summary: The transcript describes Japanese claims of the capture of Wake, bombing of Rangoon, and pressure on Hong Kong’s defenses. It also reports a Tōjō meeting with Thai representatives and argues that Japan’s attacks threaten U.S. supplies of rubber and tin.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 25, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast describes Japanese operations in the Philippines, Burma, and Hong Kong and comments on Allied war leadership.
subfiles.summary: The transcript claims renewed Luzon landings, a pincer movement toward Manila, heavy losses from an air raid on Rangoon, and the imminent defeat of Hong Kong. It includes claims about Canadian casualties and treatment of captured U.S. Marines, a Bangkok editorial urging Asian support for Japan, and commentary on the Churchill–Roosevelt conference.

subfiles.title: FBI letter forwarding December 14–16 broadcast transcripts
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards translated Tokyo radio transcripts for December 14, 15, and 16, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Forwards three translated broadcast transcripts for Berle’s information.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 14, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast claims Japanese successes in Malaya, Burma, the Philippines, and Hong Kong and reviews the war’s first week.
subfiles.summary: The transcript lists claimed Allied aircraft and ship losses, describes operations at Malayan and Burmese airfields, and reports landings and bombardments in the Philippines. A weekly review recounts the outbreak of war, the Hawaii attack, the Thailand treaty, Axis declarations, and speeches by Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 15, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports the Hong Kong ultimatum, Philippine air operations, Japanese Diet action, and a review of the first war week.
subfiles.summary: The transcript presents claims about British prisoners, U.S. aircraft losses, new Malayan landings, and operations in China. Its extended review celebrates the Pearl Harbor attack and sinking of British capital ships while casting the war as the liberation of East Asia.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 16, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast covers the Japanese Diet session, operations in Borneo and Guam, and Prime Minister Tōjō’s speech.
subfiles.summary: The transcript reports passage of emergency military appropriations and repeats claims of Japanese victories. Tōjō’s recorded address explains Japan’s rejection of U.S. demands, urges national unity and a long war effort, and calls for the Diet’s support.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about jamming Japanese shortwave broadcasts
subfiles.to: Friele, U.S. Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The Department asks whether action has been taken to jam Japanese shortwave broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Asks the embassy for the status of Japanese shortwave jamming.

subfiles.title: Brazilian response to proposed Japanese broadcast jamming
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
subfiles.about: Caffery reports Lourival Fontes’s qualified support for jamming a Japanese station in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Fontes raises questions about the method and possible Japanese reprisals.

subfiles.title: Technical instructions for jamming in Brazil
subfiles.from: Department of State, for Nelson Rockefeller
subfiles.to: Friele, U.S. Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.about: The Department proposes a local Morse signal on 15,500 kilocycles to interfere with Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Recommends a five-kilowatt transmitter, immediate jamming, and reports on its effects and any reaction.

subfiles.title: FBI letter forwarding further Tokyo broadcast transcripts
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards Tokyo broadcast transcripts for December 19, 28, and 29 and January 1, 3, and 4.
subfiles.summary: Forwards six translated radio broadcast transcripts.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 19, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast claims Japanese advances at Hong Kong and in Malaya and argues that U.S. naval power was destroyed at Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The transcript covers the Hong Kong landings, British withdrawal from Penang, air operations near Iloilo, and Japanese wartime donations. It also reports personnel changes in U.S. Pacific commands, Timor and Iran developments, and a commentary calling the United States a third-class naval power.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 28, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reviews fighting around Manila and Malaya, Hong Kong’s surrender, and Japanese and Axis celebrations.
subfiles.summary: The transcript claims Japanese forces are converging on Manila and advancing through Malaya. It recounts the occupation of Hong Kong, gives figures for Allied losses, describes Australian concerns, and includes Tokyo speeches supporting the Axis and Japan’s war effort.

subfiles.title: Station JZI program, December 29, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports pressure on Manila, advances in Malaya, and the military and economic meaning of Japan’s early gains.
subfiles.summary: The transcript claims continuing Japanese advances toward Manila and Ipoh and air raids on Singapore. It presents regional reactions, a third-week war review, extensive Allied loss figures, and the expected value of captured Borneo oil, Malayan tin, and rubber to Japan’s economy.

subfiles.title: Station JZI English program, January 1, 1942
subfiles.about: The New Year broadcast praises Japan’s military gains and its alliance with Thailand while discussing prisoners and a prolonged war.
subfiles.summary: Reception was poor. The audible material includes claims about Manila, Corregidor, Singapore, Japanese treatment of prisoners, cooperation with Thailand and other allies, and speeches presenting Japan as the champion of East Asian peoples against Britain and the United States.

subfiles.title: Station JZI English program, January 3, 1942
subfiles.about: A poorly received broadcast claims the capture of Manila and further Japanese gains in Malaya and China.
subfiles.summary: The monitor notes that severe reception problems obscure most details.

subfiles.title: Station JZI English program, January 4, 1942
subfiles.about: The broadcast celebrates the capture of Manila and predicts further Japanese success against Singapore and Allied Pacific positions.
subfiles.summary: The transcript reports Japanese claims about Manila’s occupation, Corregidor, Cavite, Singapore, Hawaii, and Allied shipping. It also describes reactions attributed to several countries and concludes with commentary portraying Manila’s fall as a major strategic and political victory.

subfiles.title: Withdrawal notice for a restricted item
subfiles.about: A form records the removal of a restricted item from the file.
subfiles.summary: Records withdrawal of an item identified with censorship and a January 28, 1942 date.

subfiles.title: Rio report on Brazilian jamming arrangements
subfiles.from: Jefferson Caffery, U.S. Embassy, Rio de Janeiro
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
subfiles.about: The embassy reports Brazilian action through the São Paulo post office on the proposed jamming effort.
subfiles.summary: Reports that the Brazilian agency is working through the São Paulo post office and promises results; page 269 is the coded transmission.

subfiles.title: Thomason forwards a report of radio calls heard in Mexico
subfiles.about: Thomason forwards Mrs. Cris Aranda’s report of radio messages allegedly sent from Japan to Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Forwards Aranda’s letter and requests its return after acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Cris Aranda’s report of radio calls
subfiles.about: Aranda relays a secondhand account of numbered radio calls allegedly sent from Japan and heard in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Describes early morning calls containing changing numbers and dollar amounts.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal to the FCC
subfiles.about: The Department sends the FCC Aranda’s report of Japanese radio calls heard in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Transmits a copy of Aranda’s April 5 letter for possible use.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Representative Thomason
subfiles.about: The Department thanks Thomason for Aranda’s report and returns his original enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges the letter, thanks Thomason, and returns Aranda’s original.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding Aranda’s report to Mexico
subfiles.about: The Department confidentially forwards Aranda’s report and copies the U.S. consulate at Ciudad Juárez.
subfiles.summary: Sends the report of Japanese radio calls heard in Mexico to the embassy and consulate.

subfiles.title: FCC acknowledgment of Aranda material
subfiles.from: James Lawrence Fly, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: The FCC acknowledges receipt of the Department’s April 29 communication and Aranda’s letter.
subfiles.summary: Thanks the Department for forwarding Aranda’s information.

subfiles.title: File note on Office of Facts and Figures broadcast excerpts
subfiles.about: A file note copies two press release excerpts based on monitored Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Records statements by Kunihiko Okura and Hisao Okumura threatening Britain and the United States.

subfiles.title: London report on Japanese broadcasts about German advances
subfiles.from: John G. Winant, U.S. Embassy, London
subfiles.about: The embassy reports British views on whether Japanese broadcasts signal a possible attack on Soviet territory.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office sees the broadcasts’ new emphasis on German gains as possible preparation for action against the Russian Maritime Province. It believes Japan would attack Vladivostok only if it judged Soviet military weakness to offer a favorable opportunity.

subfiles.title: Department response on Japanese broadcasts and Vladivostok
subfiles.about: The Department assesses the meaning of Japanese broadcasts highlighting German successes in Russia.
subfiles.summary: It considers the broadcasts insufficient evidence of an impending attack and says any decision on Vladivostok would involve wider Japanese strategy.

subfiles.title: Chongqing report on monitoring Japanese radio broadcasts
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chongqing
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Board of Economic Warfare
subfiles.about: The embassy describes Chinese monitoring of Tokyo broadcasts and requests discretion over reporting frequency.
subfiles.summary: Chinese monitoring yields Domei releases with little economic information; the embassy seeks flexibility in sending telegrams.
